title: The Face
hook: The face is the most watched part of the body and the best trained to perform, so ask what it is doing before you ask what it means.
why:
When people talk about reading someone, they usually mean reading their face. It is where we look first and longest, and it feels like a window: a smile means happy, a frown means cross, and a face that does not match the words is hiding something. The face does carry a great deal of information. It also carries more performance than any other part of the body, because it is the part everyone has been practising on since childhood.

This chapter treats the face with the respect it deserves and the caution it needs. You will learn to describe what a face is doing in terms of muscle movements before naming any feeling, to understand the two kinds of smile and the limits of telling them apart, to see faces as signals made for audiences rather than readouts of inner states, to treat the famous six expressions as posed prototypes that real faces rarely match, and to recognise how much of what we think we see in a face actually comes from the body and the situation around it. The question of whether faces speak a universal language is left to the chapter on cultural variance.

teach.h: The face is the best-trained performer.
teach.p:
The chapter on leakage and pacifiers described a gradient of control: the parts of the body people watch most are the parts people learn to manage best. The face sits at the top of that gradient. Everyone around you has been looking at your face since the day you were born, reacting to it, praising some expressions and punishing others. By adulthood, most people have very fine control over what their face shows in front of others.

Much of that control is learned through display rules, the norms about who may show which feelings, to whom and how strongly, which the chapter on cross-cultural calibration in Part VI describes. A child learns to smile at a disappointing present, a boy learns not to cry in front of other boys, a nurse learns a calm face for frightened patients, and a salesman learns a warm one for strangers.

None of this makes faces meaningless. It makes them partly deliberate. The face is not only a window onto feeling but also a channel that people use, consciously and not, to communicate, to manage their relationships and to present themselves as they wish to be seen.

For a reader, the consequence is a particular order of questions. Before asking what a face means, ask what it is doing, who it is doing it for, and how it compares with this person's usual face. A broad smile from a man who smiles at everyone tells you about his manners. A brief tightening of the mouth from a man who usually keeps his face very still may tell you more.

The most practised part of the body deserves the most careful reading, not the most confident.
teach.disconfirm: If people's facial expressions turned out to track their reported feelings closely whether or not anyone was watching, and regardless of their culture and job, the face would be less of a performer than this block claims. The studies described below suggest otherwise.

teach.h: Describe the movement before you name the feeling.
teach.p:
In 1978 Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen published the Facial Action Coding System, usually called FACS. It describes every visible movement of the face in terms of the muscles that produce it, numbered as action units. Action unit 1 raises the inner corners of the brows. Action unit 4 lowers the brows and draws them together. Action unit 6 raises the cheeks and narrows the eyes. Action unit 12 pulls the corners of the lips up and out. There are dozens more.

FACS was a quiet revolution because it separated two questions that people constantly run together: what the face did, and what that means. Trained coders using FACS can agree closely about what a face did, frame by frame, because they are describing movements, not guessing at feelings. Arguments about meaning come afterwards, and can be checked against what the person reports, what happens next and what was going on.

You do not need to learn the full system to borrow its discipline. The face plates in this book label each face with its action units, and the habit to build is simply to describe before you interpret. *Brows lowered and drawn together, lips pressed* is a description you can check. *She looked angry* is an interpretation, and it may be wrong in several ways: the movement may be concentration, the feeling may be worry, and the face may be performing for someone else.

Description also protects you from your own mood. When you are tense, an ambiguous face looks hostile. A description written in muscle terms is harder for your mood to bend.

Say what moved. Then wonder why.
teach.disconfirm: If, when you describe faces as movements first, your eventual readings turn out no more accurate than when you name feelings straight away, the extra step is not helping you. Compare a few weeks of each in your journal before deciding.

teach.h: Two smiles, and the limits of the difference.
teach.p:
In 1862 the French physician Guillaume Duchenne published photographs of faces whose muscles he had stimulated with electric currents. He noticed that a smile produced only by the muscles that pull up the corners of the mouth looked different from a smile of real enjoyment, in which the muscles around the eyes also contract, lifting the cheeks, narrowing the eyes and creasing their outer corners. The second kind came to be called the Duchenne smile.

In 1990 Ekman, Richard Davidson and Friesen found that Duchenne smiles were more often accompanied by reports of enjoyment, and by a pattern of brain activity associated with positive feeling, than smiles involving the mouth alone. The distinction entered popular culture as a way of spotting fake smiles: if the eyes do not smile, the smile is false.

Later research complicated the story. In 2009 Eva Krumhuber and Antony Manstead found that many people produced the eye movements of a Duchenne smile when they were merely posing, and other studies have found that a substantial share of people can produce Duchenne smiles deliberately on request. Strong smiles of any kind tend to push the cheeks up and narrow the eyes simply through the force of the movement. So the presence of the eye movement does not prove enjoyment, and its absence does not prove falsehood.

A smile with the mouth alone is usually not a lie at all. It is the polite smile of greeting, thanks, acknowledgment and courtesy, one of the most common and useful signals people make. Calling it fake misunderstands what it is for.

Read the difference between the two smiles as one weak clue to enjoyment, alongside the voice, the timing and the situation, never as a lie detector.
teach.disconfirm: If posed smiles almost never showed the cheek and eye movements of a Duchenne smile, and enjoyment almost always did, the distinction would be a strong clue. The research since 2009 has found the overlap too large for that.

teach.p:
In 1979 Robert Kraut and Robert Johnston watched people at a bowling alley. If facial expressions simply read out inner feelings, bowlers should smile most at the moment they see a strike. They did not. Bowlers smiled rarely while facing the pins, whatever the result, and smiled far more when they turned round to face their friends.

Similar patterns have turned up elsewhere. José-Miguel Fernández-Dols and María-Angeles Ruiz-Belda studied gold medallists at the 1992 Olympic Games and found that they smiled much more while interacting with the crowd and officials than during the moments on the podium when they were simply listening to the anthem, presumably no less happy. In 1991 Alan Fridlund found that people watching a funny video alone smiled more if they believed a friend was watching the same video in another room.

These findings support a view, developed most fully by Fridlund, that facial expressions are first of all social signals: moves in an exchange with other people, shaped by who is there, as much as expressions of what is felt. Feeling and face are connected, but loosely, and an audience tightens or loosens the connection.

For a reader, this adds a question that is easy to forget: who is this face for? A smile turned towards a boss, a frown aimed at a child, a look of concern held while others are watching may be telling you more about the relationship than about the feeling. A face shown when the person thinks no one is looking is telling you something different again.

Before reading a face, find its audience.
teach.disconfirm: If people's expressions turned out to be just as strong and frequent when they were truly alone as when others were present, the audience view would be wrong. The studies described here found clear differences, but check what you see in your own life before relying on them.

teach.h: The six faces are posed, and real faces rarely match them.
teach.p:
Most people have seen the six classic faces of emotion: happiness, surprise, fear, anger, disgust and sadness. They appear in textbooks, training courses and software, and the face plate in this chapter shows them with their action units. They are useful as a vocabulary. They are also, almost without exception, posed: actors or volunteers were asked to make the faces, and the most recognisable versions were chosen.

Real faces in real situations rarely look like this. Studies that record people during genuine emotional events find that the full configurations appear much less often than the textbook suggests. People feeling intense fear often show only part of the fear face, or a different face entirely. People who are angry may frown, or smile, or show nothing. The review led by Lisa Feldman Barrett in 2019, described in the chapter on ethics in Part VI, concluded that the link between particular facial configurations and particular emotions is far weaker and more variable than the classic picture assumed.

There is a long-running scientific argument here, between researchers who see a small set of universal emotional expressions and those who see expressions as far more variable and constructed from context. The chapter on cultural variance lays out that debate. For practical reading, both sides agree on enough: a given face can arise from many feelings, a given feeling can produce many faces, and the prototype is the exception rather than the rule.

So use the six faces to name movements, not to diagnose people. When you see part of a configuration, you have seen a movement. The meaning still has to be found.
teach.disconfirm: If recordings of people during real emotional events regularly showed the full prototype faces for the emotions they reported, the six faces would be better guides than this block allows. The research reviewed in 2019 found them to be the exception.
teach.pullQuote: A given face can arise from many feelings, and a given feeling can produce many faces.

teach.h: The body and the situation do more than the face.
teach.p:
In 2012 Hillel Aviezer, Yaacov Trope and Alexander Todorov showed people photographs of professional tennis players at the moment they had won or lost a crucial point. When people saw the whole picture, they could easily tell winners from losers. When they saw only the faces, they could not: intense joy and intense despair produced faces so similar, contorted, open-mouthed and strained, that people's judgments were close to chance. When people saw only the bodies, they were accurate.

The most revealing part came next. When the researchers swapped faces between winning and losing bodies, people's judgments followed the body, yet they reported that they had been reading the face. We believe we read faces, and much of the time we are reading everything around them.

The chapter on clusters and congruence described a related finding: the same face reads as disgust on one body and anger on another. Together, these results suggest that at moments of strong feeling especially, the face is a poor witness on its own. Posture, hands, voice, words and the situation carry much of the information.

This is good news for the reader who has learned the rest of this book. The baseline, the cluster, the timing and the context are not extras to be checked after reading the face. They are often where the reading actually comes from. A face seen without them is a face half-seen.

When a face seems to tell you everything, look at what surrounds it.
teach.disconfirm: If people judging isolated faces of intense emotion could tell positive from negative as accurately as people judging whole scenes, the face would be a better witness than this block claims. In the tennis study they could not.

teach.h: Read faces well, and leave them alone.
teach.p:
Bring the chapter together into a way of reading a face. First, know the resting face. Faces at rest differ a great deal. Some people's brows sit low and their mouth turns down slightly when they are relaxed, and they spend their lives being asked what is wrong. Some conditions reduce facial movement altogether: Parkinson's disease often flattens the face, facial palsy can freeze one side, and cosmetic injections can still the forehead. A still or stern face may be the person's baseline, not their mood.

Second, describe what moved, in action units or plain words. Third, note the timing: what had just happened? Fourth, find the audience: who was the face for? Fifth, read it with the body, the voice and the situation, as the tennis study suggests. Only then form a hypothesis, with a rival, and if it matters, ask about the moment, never about the face.

And leave people's faces alone. Telling someone to smile, asking why they look so cross, or commenting on a face they did not mean you to see turns their face into your business. People whose resting faces look stern hear such comments constantly, and they are wearing. A face is often the one part of themselves people feel least able to control in public.

The best readers of faces are the ones people feel comfortable being seen by. They notice a great deal and say very little about faces at all.
teach.disconfirm: If commenting on people's expressions made them more at ease and more open with you, by their own account, the advice to leave faces alone would be wrong for your relationships. Ask two people you trust how such comments land before deciding.

poseGallery.dontCaption: 'The smile didn't reach his eyes, so he's fake.'
poseGallery.annotation: Polite smiles are common, useful and honest. Duchenne markers can be produced on purpose, so they are weak clues either way.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Studying a face for the truth.

poseGallery.doCaption: Leaving his face alone, and asking how his day was.
poseGallery.annotation: Comments on people's faces turn them into your business. Ask about the situation if you are concerned, not about the face.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading a stern resting face as anger.

poseGallery.annotation: The face is one channel among several, and the best trained to perform. Read it with the voice, the body and the situation.

caseStudy:
Marcus, forty-four, runs a small restaurant. When he hires Ana as head chef, the front-of-house staff start avoiding the kitchen. Ana, they say, is always annoyed. Marcus sees what they mean. Ana's face at rest has low, straight brows and a mouth that turns slightly down, and when she is working it looks fierce.

Before saying anything, Marcus tries the habit he has been practising: describe before interpreting. Over a week he watches her face during service and writes down what moves. Her brows lower and draw together whenever she is checking a plate or timing several pans, and relax when she hands the plate over. Her lips press together when an order comes in wrong. When she talks with her sous-chef about a new dish, her cheeks lift, her eyes crease and she laughs often. With customers who come to the pass to thank her, she gives a small smile with the mouth alone and goes back to work.

His notes describe a person who concentrates hard, dislikes mistakes, enjoys food and is polite but reserved with strangers. None of it says annoyed. He asks her, carefully, whether the kitchen is going all right for her. She says it is the best job she has had. Then she laughs and says she has been told her whole life that she looks cross, and that a previous boss used to tell her to smile.

Marcus tells his front-of-house manager what he has noticed, in terms of what Ana's face does at work, without any suggestion that Ana needs to change. He also asks the staff to bring problems to the pass between rushes, when her brows are not down over six pans at once.

A month later, a waiter tells him Ana is actually funny. Marcus says nothing about faces at all.
observe: Watch someone you know well at rest, when they think no one is looking, and describe their resting face in terms of what the brows, eyes and mouth are doing.
Notice one smile today and describe it as movements: did the cheeks lift, did the eyes crease, who was it for?
Watch a few seconds of a sporting celebration or a moment of defeat with the face covered, and then with only the face visible, and compare what you can tell.

drills.name: Movements First
steps: Open the face plates in the pose library and, for each face, write what moved, without naming any feeling.
Choose a recorded interview and pause it at five moments when the face changed.
For each moment, write the movement in plain words or action units.
Then write two or three feelings or states that could produce that movement.
Note which context, such as what had just been said, would help you choose between them.
variations: Do the same with a recorded conversation in a language you do not speak, so that the words cannot guide your labels.
Choose five moments from a film rather than an interview, and compare an actor's faces with the posed plates.
Ask a friend to make five faces for you, and describe each one in movements before they tell you what they meant.

drills.name: Smile Census
steps: Over one day, notice ten smiles, from strangers, colleagues and people close to you.
For each, note whether the cheeks lifted and the eyes creased, or only the mouth moved.
Note who the smile was aimed at and what had just happened.
Mark any smile you would previously have called fake.
Write one sentence about what the polite smiles were doing.
variations: Repeat the census on a different day and in a different setting, such as a family event, and compare the proportions.
Add a column for whether the smile changed when its audience looked away, and how quickly it returned when they looked back.

drills.name: Find the Audience
steps: In a social setting, choose three moments when someone's face changed markedly.
For each, note who was looking at them at the time.
Note whether their face changed again when they turned to someone else or looked away from the group.
Write what each face seemed to be saying to its audience.
Write one rival reading for each.
variations: Do it at a sporting event or in a pub showing a match, where faces change constantly and the audience shifts.
Watch your own face in a video call thumbnail and note how it changes when you think nobody is looking at you.

drills.name: Face Hidden, Face Alone
steps: Find photographs or short clips of athletes at moments of victory and defeat.
Cover the faces and judge from the bodies which moments are victories.
Then look only at the faces, with the bodies covered, and judge again.
Check your answers.
Write down how much of your judgment depended on the body.
variations: Try the same exercise with photographs of people receiving good and bad news, such as election nights or exam results.
Ask a friend to do it blind, without knowing the outcomes, and compare their accuracy with yours.

drills.name: Resting Faces
steps: Choose three people you see often and recall their faces at rest.
Describe each resting face in terms of brows, eyes and mouth.
Note any impression of their mood or character that you formed from it.
Check each impression against what you actually know about them.
Write one change you would now notice as meaningful for each of the three.
variations: Ask one person you trust to describe your own resting face in plain terms, and compare it with how you imagine it.
Look at a few unposed photographs of yourself and write what a stranger might read into your face.

quiz.q: A colleague smiles at you warmly, but his cheeks do not lift and his eyes do not crease. What does the research best support?
options: His smile is fake, and he does not mean anything that he is saying to you
He is hiding a dislike of you behind a polite face, so watch him closely from now on
It may be a polite social smile, which is common and is not a lie
He is anxious about something and covering it with a smile for now
quiz.explain: Smiles with the mouth alone are the everyday smiles of courtesy and acknowledgment. Eye and cheek movements are a weak clue to enjoyment, since people can produce them on purpose and strong smiles produce them anyway.

quiz.q: In Kraut and Johnston's study of people at a bowling alley, when did bowlers smile most?
options: When they turned round to face their friends, rather than the pins
At the moment the ball struck the pins, whatever their final score
Only after a poor roll, as a way of covering their embarrassment
When they were alone in the lane and nobody else was watching them
quiz.explain: Bowlers smiled rarely at the pins, even after a strike, and often when facing their friends. Faces are shaped by their audience as much as by feeling.

quiz.q: What does the Facial Action Coding System describe?
options: The emotions a person's face is showing at any given moment
Which facial expressions are honest and which ones are faked
The personality types that tend to go with different faces
The visible movements of the face, as numbered action units
quiz.explain: FACS separates what the face did from what it means. Coders can agree closely about movements; meaning is a separate question to be checked against context and what the person says.

quiz.q: A new team member's resting face has low brows and a downturned mouth, and colleagues assume she is always annoyed. What fits this chapter?
options: Ask her gently whether something at work is making her unhappy
Learn her resting face as her baseline, and look for changes from it
Suggest to her privately that she try to smile more in the office
Tell colleagues that she is shy and that they should make allowances
quiz.explain: Resting faces vary widely, and a stern one is a baseline, not a mood. Changes from it carry the information. Telling someone to smile makes their face your business.

quiz.q: What did Aviezer, Trope and Todorov find using photographs of tennis players winning and losing points?
options: From the faces alone, people could easily tell which player had won each point
People could not tell winners from losers by face alone, but could by body
Only the players' voices, not faces or bodies, revealed who had won
Faces and bodies were equally hard to read at moments of high emotion
quiz.explain: Intense joy and despair produced near-identical faces, and judgments of the faces alone were close to chance. People followed the body while believing they were reading the face.

quiz.q: At dinner, a friend smiles broadly all through a story about losing his job. What is the most useful approach?
options: Remember faces are for audiences, and later, alone, ask how he is doing
Take the smile at face value, since he is clearly coping with it well
Tell him gently that his smile looks forced and he does not need to pretend
Assume he is in denial and suggest that he should see a counsellor
quiz.explain: A smile at a dinner table may be for the table: courtesy, pride, a way to tell the story. A quiet question later, without an audience, lets him say how he really is, without anyone commenting on his face.

quiz.q: What did Fernández-Dols and Ruiz-Belda find when they studied gold medallists at their award ceremonies?
options: The medallists smiled most while standing alone on the podium as their anthem was played
The medallists smiled mostly while interacting with others, not while listening to the anthem
The medallists rarely smiled at all, since the pressure of the occasion had exhausted them
The medallists smiled equally throughout, which showed that smiles simply express happiness
quiz.explain: The champions, presumably no less happy during the anthem, smiled far more when interacting with the crowd and officials. Like Kraut and Johnston's bowlers, they suggest that smiles are aimed at audiences as much as they express feeling.

quiz.q: A colleague says that anyone whose smile does not crease the eyes is being insincere. What does this chapter suggest?
options: She is right, because the eye crease cannot be produced deliberately and so proves sincerity
She is right about strangers, though not about people whom you have known for a long time
Polite smiles without the eye crease are ordinary social signals, and many people can fake the crease
She is wrong, because the eyes play no part at all in how smiles of enjoyment actually look
quiz.explain: Most smiles in a day are social smiles, and they are not lies. And because many people can produce the eye-creasing smile on purpose, its presence or absence is a poor guide to sincerity.

quiz.q: Over a year, a relative's face has become much less expressive, though he says he feels fine. What fits this chapter best?
options: Conclude that he has become depressed and arrange for him to see a counsellor as soon as possible
Treat it as distance from the family, and give him more space until he chooses to reconnect
Assume that it is just ageing, since faces always become much less expressive as people grow older
Note the change, and gently suggest he mentions it to his doctor, without guessing at a cause
quiz.explain: Reduced facial movement can come from many things, including conditions that affect the nerves and muscles of the face. A sustained change in baseline is worth noticing and passing to someone qualified, not diagnosing at the table.

quiz.q: What did Aviezer, Trope and Todorov find when people judged tennis players' faces without their bodies?
options: They could not reliably tell winners from losers from the faces alone, but could from the bodies
They could tell winners from losers far more accurately from the faces than from the whole picture
They judged every face as joyful, because the players' mouths were open wide at those moments
They could tell winners from losers only when the faces were shown at the moment of the point
quiz.explain: At moments of intense feeling, joy and despair produced faces so similar that people judged them near chance. The bodies, and the situation, carried the information the faces did not.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific face you have misjudged: a resting face you read as unfriendly, a smile you called fake, or an expression you were sure you understood. Describe what the face actually did, in terms of movement. Who was the face for at that moment, and what were the body, voice and situation doing? What do you now think the face meant, and what would you need to have seen or asked to know for certain?
reflection.guidance: Many people find their example in someone whose resting face looks stern or flat, and realise that they formed a lasting impression of the person from it. Try to describe the movement in the terms of the face plates, brows, lids, cheeks, mouth, before writing any feeling. The last question is the important one: what would have let you check?

failureMode: The commonest failure is to treat the face as a window rather than a performer, taking every expression at face value or, at the other extreme, treating every polite smile as a lie. The second is to read the six textbook faces into real faces that only partly resemble them. The third is to read faces without their surroundings, forgetting that at moments of strong feeling the body and the situation often carry more information than the face. The fourth is to judge people by their resting faces, especially when a condition or simple anatomy gives them a stern or flat look. And the most common social failure is commenting on faces: telling people to smile, asking why they look cross. Describe, find the audience, read the whole person, and leave their face alone.

moreCases.title: "Give us a smile"
moreCases.scene:
Darren, thirty-eight, supervises the loading bay at a builders' merchant. He is good at the job: calm under pressure, fair with his team, quick to spot when a delivery has been loaded wrong. His face at rest has heavy, low brows and a mouth that turns slightly down. When he concentrates, which is most of the working day, the brows draw together.

The new area manager, visiting for the first time, watches Darren for half an hour and then takes him aside. Customers, she says, might find him intimidating. Could he try to look a bit friendlier? Smile more? Darren is taken aback. He has been told this before, by teachers, by girlfriends, by a stranger in a pub who once asked him what his problem was. He goes back to the bay and spends the afternoon trying to hold a pleasant expression while checking pallets, which makes him slower and more irritable, and his face, if anything, more strained.

At the end of the day one of his team, who has worked with him for six years, asks whether he is all right. He has never seen Darren look so tense. The customers who come to that bay every week, most of them builders who have known Darren for years, have never mentioned his face at all. They mention that he is the only one who loads the vans properly.

The area manager's report on the visit includes a line about the loading bay: friendly service could be improved. Darren reads it and says nothing, but his wife notices that for weeks afterwards he checks his face in the van mirror before he gets out at work.
moreCases.misread:
The area manager read Darren's resting face as a mood, and then as a problem with how he treated people, on the strength of half an hour's observation. She had no baseline for him, no evidence from his customers, and no account of what his face does when he is relaxed, pleased or annoyed. She simply saw a face that looked stern to her and assumed it meant what it would mean on her own face.

Her request also put Darren in an impossible position: to keep doing the job well, while managing a face that was not doing anything wrong.
moreCases.betterRead:
The careful reading begins with the resting face. Some people's brows sit low and their mouths turn down when they are perfectly content, and they spend their lives being asked what is wrong. Describing the movement rather than naming the feeling, as FACS encourages, would have shown the area manager a man whose brows lowered when he checked loads and relaxed when he talked to drivers. If she had a genuine concern about how customers felt, she could have asked the customers, or watched Darren talk to one. Asking a man to perform a smile while he works asks him to manage his face instead of doing his job, and it tells him that the face he was born with is a fault.

If Darren's face really did put a customer off, the fix would be a conversation, not a smile: a word of greeting, a joke with a regular, the kind of warmth that lives in what he says and does rather than in the set of his brows.

moreCases.title: The smile at the wake
moreCases.scene:
Siobhan's husband, Declan, died suddenly at fifty-six. At the wake, held at their home, she stands at the door for most of the afternoon greeting people. She smiles at each of them, warmly, takes their hands, thanks them for coming, asks after their children. Several times she laughs at a story someone tells about Declan. Her face is mostly bright.

Across the room, Declan's brother, Gerry, watches her with growing unease, and later says to his wife that Siobhan does not seem very cut up. Gerry's wife tells him not to be ridiculous. But the remark gets back to Siobhan, as remarks at wakes do, and it hurts her more than almost anything else that week. That night, when the last guest has gone, she sits on the floor of the kitchen and cannot get up for an hour.

Siobhan's sister, who stood beside her for part of the afternoon, saw something Gerry did not: that each time a guest moved away from the door, Siobhan's smile fell away completely for a second or two before the next person arrived, and that she held the doorframe with one hand the whole time.

Two weeks later, when Siobhan's friend asks how she managed that afternoon, she says she does not really remember it. She remembers only that she wanted everyone who loved Declan to feel welcome in his house, and that she would have time to cry later.
moreCases.misread:
Gerry read Siobhan's smiles as a direct readout of her feeling: a smiling face means a happy enough person, so a smiling widow must not be grieving much. He took no account of who the smiles were for, or of what a host at a wake is doing with her face.

And having made the reading, Gerry said it aloud in a room full of people, where it was certain to travel, about a woman who had lost her husband four days earlier.
moreCases.betterRead:
Kraut and Johnston's bowlers and Fernández-Dols and Ruiz-Belda's Olympic champions both show that faces are made for audiences: people smile far more when they are interacting with others than when they are alone with their feelings. A widow at the door of her own wake is hosting, thanking and reassuring, and the smile is part of that work. Many grieving people describe exactly this: smiling for hours for the sake of the people who came, and falling apart when they leave. A careful observer reads the smile as a message to the guests, not a report on the heart, and offers what Gerry did not: a quiet word, a hand on the arm, an offer to take a turn at the door.

Gerry, to his credit, apologised a month later, after his own wife pointed out that he had smiled through most of his mother's funeral.

moreCases.title: The face that went quiet
moreCases.scene:
Over a year, Lauren notices that her father's face has changed. At family dinners he still laughs at the grandchildren, but his face barely moves when he does; the laugh is in his voice and shoulders, not his cheeks. He blinks less. When he listens to her, his expression stays fixed, so that she often cannot tell whether he is interested, bored or hurt. Her brother thinks their father has become distant since he retired, and perhaps depressed. Her mother says he is just tired.

Lauren also notices that his handwriting on birthday cards has become smaller, and that his right hand has a slight tremor at rest which stops when he reaches for his cup. She does not know what these things mean, and she is careful not to make a diagnosis at the dinner table. But she suggests to her mother that he might mention the changes to his GP, and offers to go with him.

Lauren's brother, Rob, lives two hours away and sees their father once a month. Each visit he finds his father harder to read, and each visit he leaves a little earlier. He tells Lauren that their father never asks him anything any more and seems not to care what he says. When Lauren mentions the handwriting and the tremor, Rob says that she is looking for problems, and that some people simply get quieter with age.
moreCases.misread:
Her brother read the stillness of their father's face as a change of mood: distance, low spirits, a loss of interest in the family. That is the natural reading if the face is a window onto feeling. It led him to take his father's flat expressions personally, and to visit less.

Their mother, meanwhile, explained everything by tiredness, which was kinder but no more accurate, and which kept the family from asking the right question for months.
moreCases.betterRead:
The face is a set of muscles controlled by the brain, and anything that affects that control can change what the face shows without any change in feeling. Parkinson's disease often reduces facial movement, which clinicians call hypomimia, and so can strokes, facial palsy, some medications and depression itself. A reader cannot tell which from across a table, and should not try. What Lauren did was the right use of this chapter: notice a sustained change in someone's baseline, describe it plainly, notice what else had changed alongside it, and point towards someone qualified to look. Her father was diagnosed with Parkinson's two months later. Knowing why his face had gone quiet changed how the whole family heard his laugh.

She also kept her observations to the facts she could see, and left the meaning to the doctor. That restraint is the hardest part of reading someone you love, because the worry pulls you towards a conclusion.

moreCases.title: The candidate who would not stop smiling
moreCases.scene:
Femi is interviewed for a graduate role in a bank by a panel of three. He smiles almost continuously: when he is introduced, while he listens to each question, while he answers, and between sentences. He laughs briefly after several of his own answers. The smiles are broad, but his cheeks barely lift and his eyes do not crease; they look, to one panel member, painted on. That panel member writes that the candidate seemed nervous and not entirely serious, and possibly insincere.

A second panel member, Ruth, scores the content of Femi's answers against the agreed criteria and finds them strong, particularly on a question about a team project that went wrong. Ruth also notices that the smile drops for a moment each time a question begins, as he concentrates, and returns as soon as he starts to answer.

Ruth's own notes on Femi's smile are a single line: smiled throughout, consistent with nerves, drops while he listens to questions. Everything else on her sheet is about what he said.

After the interview the first panel member says that Femi's constant smiling made it hard to take him seriously. Ruth asks which of his answers he would mark down, and he cannot name one.
moreCases.misread:
The first panel member read the non-Duchenne smile as fakery and the frequency of smiling as a lack of seriousness. Both readings treat the smile as a message about the candidate's honesty and character, rather than as a common response to being nervous and wanting to be liked.

The same panel member had rated an earlier candidate highly for being warm and natural, a candidate whose cheeks lifted when he smiled and whose answers were thin.
moreCases.betterRead:
Smiles that do not involve the eyes are not lies. They are the ordinary smiles of politeness, appeasement and nerves, and an interview is a setting that produces all three in abundance. Krumhuber and Manstead, whose work is listed at the end of this chapter, found that even the so-called genuine smile can be produced deliberately by many people, so the eye-crease test is a poor lie detector in either direction. Ruth's approach was the sound one: score what was said against criteria set in advance, and treat the smile as information about the candidate's state in a stressful room, not as evidence about his character. Femi was offered the job, and his manager later described him as one of the most conscientious people on the team.

Femi's smile, in other words, was doing exactly what nervous smiles do: asking the room to be kind to him. Reading it as insincerity punished him for the most ordinary of requests.

workedReading.title: The face at the announcement
workedReading.scene:
You and your partner have just told your oldest friend, Tom, over dinner at his flat, that you are getting married. Tom's face changes in the second after you say it. His brows rise, his eyes widen a little, the corners of his mouth pull up into a smile, and at the same time his lips press together briefly. Then he says, "That's brilliant, mate," gets up, hugs you both, and goes to the kitchen to find a bottle of something. He is gone for a couple of minutes.

You are slightly nervous about telling him. He is the friend you have known longest, and you know that the last year has been hard for him. You have been watching his face more closely than you meant to.

When he comes back with the bottle and three glasses, he is grinning, and asks how you proposed.

steps.label: Know the resting face
steps.text:
You have known Tom for twenty years. His face at rest is open and mobile. He smiles easily, his eyebrows are expressive, and when he is surprised he usually laughs out loud. He has a habit of pressing his lips together when he is about to say something and decides not to. That last habit matters: you have a baseline for the lip press, and it is not a sign of displeasure in him.

Without that baseline, the lip press might look like the most important movement of the moment. With it, it is Tom being Tom, and the question becomes what he decided not to say.

steps.label: Describe the movements
steps.text:
In the plain terms FACS encourages: brows raised, eyes widened slightly, lip corners pulled up, lips pressed together for a moment, then a full smile with cheeks lifting as he stood to hug you. You resist the urge to label any of it yet. Written this way, it looks like several things happening at once, which is common at news.

Describing it this way also reveals that the movements came in a sequence rather than all at once. Sequences often tell you more than any single frame: first the surprise, then the smile, then the moment of holding something back.

Plain description also protects you from your own nerves. You had been half expecting a reaction, and a nervous observer will find one in any face.

steps.label: Ask who the face was for
steps.text:
Faces are made for audiences, as Kraut and Johnston showed. The first movements came before he had time to arrange anything, in the second after the news. The smile with lifted cheeks came as he stood and moved towards you, when he was greeting you. The trip to the kitchen took him out of view, where his face was nobody's business but his own.

This step is easy to skip because the face feels like a window. Asking who it was for turns it back into what it mostly is: a message to the people present, shaped by what the sender wants them to know.

The kitchen, in particular, tells you something. People often step out of a room at exactly the moment a feeling needs somewhere to go, and coming back a few minutes later with a bottle is a graceful way to do it.

steps.label: Read with body and situation
steps.text:
Aviezer's tennis players showed that the body and the situation often tell you more than the face. Tom's body moved towards you at once and hugged you both warmly. The situation is good news from old friends, delivered in his own home. He is single, and has been since a long relationship ended last year. That last fact is part of the situation too.

The body, in other words, was unambiguous where the face was mixed. A man who did not want to celebrate would not have been on his feet and hugging you within two seconds.

steps.label: Hold several readings
steps.text:
The faces fit surprise, plainly. They fit happiness, plainly. The lip press, given his habit, fits a man deciding not to say something: perhaps a joke, perhaps something about his own situation, perhaps a question. The trip to the kitchen fits fetching a bottle, and also fits taking a moment alone. None of this suggests he is not glad for you.

It helps to say the readings to yourself in ordinary words: he is surprised and pleased for us, and it may have brushed against something of his own. Put that way, it does not sound like a problem. It sounds like a friend.

Holding several readings at once is uncomfortable, and the temptation is to settle on the one that worries you most. Resist it. Nothing yet requires you to choose.

steps.label: Decide what, if anything, to do
steps.text:
There is nothing to fix and nothing to confront. If you sense that the news touched something for him, the kind move is not to name it at the table. It might be, later in the evening or on another day, to ask him how he is doing more generally, and to make sure the wedding plans include him in a way that matters, such as asking him to be best man if that was always going to happen.

What you should not do is ask him at the table whether he is really happy for you. That question would force him either to perform happiness more convincingly or to say something about his own life in front of your partner, and he deserves the chance to choose.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Late in the evening, on the balcony, Tom says he is genuinely thrilled, and also that it made him realise how much he had hoped to be in the same place by now. He had gone to the kitchen, he says, to have a quiet word with himself. Nothing in his face had been false. It had been a happy face for you and a private moment for him, in that order, and the order was a kindness.

It is worth noticing how little of this the face alone would have told you, and how much of it came from knowing Tom, his habits and his year.

And it is worth noticing how close you came to spoiling it. If you had asked at the table whether he was really happy, you would have pulled his private moment into public before he was ready.

moreFailures.title: Running a fake-smile detector
moreFailures.body:
Once people learn about the Duchenne smile, many start sorting every smile they see into real and fake, and treating the second kind as insincerity. This is a mistake in both directions. Most of the smiles anyone produces in a day are social smiles, made to greet, thank, reassure, apologise or ease a moment, and they are no more lies than saying please is. And, as Krumhuber and Manstead found, many people can produce the eye-creasing smile deliberately, so its presence proves no more than its absence. A reader who marks a colleague down for a polite smile has not caught a liar. He has noticed that she was being polite.

If you want to know whether someone is pleased, the smile is weak evidence either way. Their words, their actions over time and what they choose to do next tell you far more.

It is also worth remembering that people from some backgrounds are taught to smile at strangers and authority as a matter of respect, so the polite smile you are tempted to call false may be good manners from home.

moreFailures.title: Reading stillness that comes from somewhere else
moreFailures.body:
A still face is not always a feeling. Cosmetic injections that relax the forehead remove the brow movements that signal worry, surprise and sympathy. Facial palsy can freeze one side of the face. Parkinson's disease, some strokes and some medications reduce expression across the whole face. Some people have simply grown up in families or cultures where the face is kept calm in company. Before you read a still face as coldness, low mood or disapproval, consider whether the face can move as much as you expect, and whether its stillness has always been part of how this person looks. Part V's chapter on disability describes how people with facial paralysis are routinely misread as less happy than they are.

If you are the person with the still face, it can help to tell people what they might be missing: that you have a condition that limits your expressions, and that they will hear more in your voice.

And when the stillness is new, as in Lauren's father, it is worth treating as a change in baseline, which deserves a gentle question and perhaps a doctor, rather than as a change in how someone feels about you.

moreFailures.title: Assuming your own face is neutral
moreFailures.body:
Most people have little idea what their face looks like at rest, because they almost never see it except in mirrors, where they arrange it. A man who thinks he looks calm may look stern, sad or bored to others, and he will be puzzled when people react to a mood he does not have. The drills in this chapter include looking at your own resting face, which most readers find surprising. You cannot change the face you were born with, and you should not have to. But knowing how it reads lets you add a word where it helps, such as telling a new team that you look serious when you concentrate and are actually perfectly happy.

It is also worth knowing how your face changes when you are tired, stressed or concentrating, because those are the moments when others are most likely to read it as a mood aimed at them.

moreFailures.title: Turning your face into a uniform
moreFailures.body:
Some jobs, and some advice, encourage people to hold a pleasant expression at all times: in customer service, in sales, in front of a team. Part V's chapter on code-switching describes research suggesting that displaying feelings you do not have, all day, is linked with exhaustion. A face held in a permanent smile also stops carrying information, so that colleagues cannot tell when you are actually pleased. Let your face do what it does. Smile when something warrants it, show concern when someone is upset, and accept that, in between, your face will rest wherever it rests.

There is a difference between warmth and a uniform. Warmth is a response to someone; a uniform is worn regardless of who is there, and people can usually tell which one they are getting.

Leaders, in particular, often believe they must keep a positive face whatever is happening. Teams usually trust a leader more when his face shows that he takes bad news seriously, and less when it stays bright through everything.

questions.q: Are the six basic emotions really universal?
questions.a:
This is one of the longest-running debates in psychology. Paul Ekman and his colleagues argued that a small set of facial expressions is recognised across cultures, including in isolated communities with little contact with Western media. Others, notably Lisa Feldman Barrett and colleagues, have argued that these studies relied on posed faces and forced choices that inflated agreement, and that people in different cultures do not reliably produce or recognise the same faces for the same feelings. Part I's chapter on cultural variance looks at the evidence in detail. For practical reading, the safest position is that the face carries some broadly shared signals, that culture shapes when and how they are shown, and that real faces rarely match the textbook versions.

For readers, this means treating the face plates in this book as a vocabulary, not a dictionary. They help you describe what you see; they do not tell you what it means in a particular person on a particular day.

In daily life, this matters less than the debate suggests. Whatever the answer about universality, a reader who describes what he sees and checks it against context will misread fewer faces than one who trusts a chart.

questions.q: Can people fake a genuine smile?
questions.a:
Many can, at least some of the time. The Duchenne smile, in which the cheeks lift and the eyes crease, was long treated as a mark of real enjoyment that could not be produced on demand. Krumhuber and Manstead found that people asked to pose smiles often produced the eye-creasing version too, and other researchers have found the same. Actors, salespeople and politicians do it routinely. The eye crease is still more common in spontaneous smiles of enjoyment than in polite ones, so it carries some information, but not enough to sort the honest from the dishonest. Read smiles in context: who they were for, what had just happened, and what the rest of the body was doing.

The same is true of the frown, the raised brows and every other expression: each can be produced on purpose by someone who has had reason to practise, and faces at work are often among the most practised of all.

questions.q: Why do people keep telling me I look angry when I'm not?
questions.a:
Probably because your face at rest has features that resemble an expression of anger: brows that sit low or close together, a mouth that turns down slightly, or a habit of frowning when you concentrate. Observers read resting faces as if they were expressions, and they do it quickly and without thinking. It is not your fault, and you do not need to fix it by performing cheerfulness. It can help to know which features people are reacting to, by looking at a few unposed photographs of yourself, and to say something to new colleagues or teams: that you look serious when you are thinking and that they should ask rather than guess. Most people are relieved to be told.

If the misreadings cause real problems at work, it is reasonable to raise them with a manager in those terms: that your face is being read as a mood you do not have, and that you would like people to judge you on what you do.

Some people find it helps to notice when the misreadings happen. If it is mostly when you are concentrating, a simple sentence at the start of a meeting, such as asking people not to mind your thinking face, does more than any amount of effort to look pleasant.

questions.q: Should I smile more at work?
questions.a:
Smile when you mean it, and when a moment calls for warmth: greeting someone, thanking them, reassuring a nervous colleague. Smiles do help people feel welcome, and a face that never softens can be hard to approach. But a smile held on purpose for hours is work, and research on emotional labour links that kind of work with exhaustion. It also makes your face less informative, because people cannot tell your real pleasure from your default. If you are a leader, the moments that matter most are often not smiles at all, but a face that shows concern when someone brings you bad news, and that stays steady while they say it.

A practical test is whether the people who work with you can tell when you are genuinely pleased. If they cannot, because your face is always pleasant, your warmth has stopped carrying information.

questions.q: How much does a face mask or sunglasses change what people can read?
questions.a:
A great deal. Covering the mouth removes most of the information about smiles and some about disgust and sadness; covering the eyes removes much of what signals surprise, fear and the warmth of a real smile. During the pandemic, many people discovered how much they had been relying on the lower face without knowing it, and research from that period found that masks made emotions noticeably harder to read. People adapt by leaning more on the eyes, the voice and the body. If you wear a mask or dark glasses in a conversation that matters, say more out loud: thank people in words, say when you are joking, and say when you are pleased.

The same applies to video calls with the camera off, where the whole face disappears: say aloud the reactions your face would usually carry.

questions.q: Is it wrong to read someone's face without telling them?
questions.a:
Not in itself. Everyone reads faces all the time; it is how conversation works. The ethical line in this book is not between noticing and not noticing, but in what you do with what you notice. Using a face to decide how gently to speak, when to pause or whether to ask how someone is, is ordinary care. Using it to catch someone out, to tell them what they really feel, or to make judgments about their honesty or character that you would not make from their words, is where reading becomes something else. If you would be uncomfortable explaining to someone how you used their face, think again about how you are using it.

A simple version of the test is to imagine the person overhearing you describe their face to someone else. If they would feel understood, you are probably fine. If they would feel watched, you have gone too far.

watch.title: Are there universal expressions of emotion?
watch.notice: A short lesson on the long debate over whether facial expressions mean the same thing everywhere. Notice the evidence on each side, and how it fits the chapter's middle path.

reviewPrompt: Describe three faces this week in terms of what moved before naming any feeling, and note who each face was for.
